2611.08953.abstract: We present multi-epoch system noise temperature measurements of a 19 element hexagonal room-temperature phased array feed (PAF) using a modified Y-factor method. A Python-based pipeline with iterative channel calibration and maxSNR beam forming is developed to do data reduction, and a covariance-based decomposition scheme is proposed to extract mutual coupling noise temperature Tmc. Long-term observations from March to June 2026 capture temporal receiver noise drift mainly induced by LNA temperature variations. Within the 1.37-1.47 GHz operating band, the measured beam equivalent system noise temperature of the PAF is about 73-89 K. The measured Tmc baseline ranges from about 2 K to 8 K, while under thermal loading, the resonant peak of Tmc can increase to more than 20 K. The baseline of Tmc is consistent with the S-parameter mea surements, which show the Tmc of the full array ranges less than 10.7 K. The baseline fluctuation of Tmc most likely arises from the superposition of thermal and non-thermal components of the spatial electromagnetic fields. A detachable stainless steel shield is deployed to quantify sidelobe spillover noise, and comparative tests show unshielded en vironmental interference increases receiver noise temperature by over 60 K. The proposed measurements and data processing framework provides a practical reference for noise per formance characterization of ground-based radio telescope PAF prototypes.

2611.09308.abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) photodesorption regulates the partitioning of water between interstellar ice mantles and the gas phase, yet laboratory yields are generally measured on planar substrates rather than on surfaces representative of cosmic dust. We investigate how grain morphology affects UV photodesorption from thin H$_2$O ice films of 2-6 monolayers deposited on planar gold and olivine, soot nanoparticles, and olivine microparticles. Samples were irradiated at 12 and 60 K with a microwave-discharge hydrogen lamp, and ice depletion was monitored by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and reflection-absorption infrared spectroscopy. On planar gold, the photodesorption yield increases approximately linearly with ice coverage, from $\sim5\times10^{-4}$ to $\sim2\times10^{-3}$ molecule photon$^{-1}$ between 2 and 6 monolayers, consistent with increasing UV absorption in optically thin ice; planar olivine gives comparable yields. In contrast, photodesorption is suppressed on particulate olivine and, more strongly, on soot, where yields are up to a factor of $\sim40$ lower than on gold at 12 K. Both experimental techniques confirm the strong suppression of ice depletion on soot. These results show that UV photodesorption depends not only on ice coverage but also strongly on grain morphology. The pronounced suppression on soot may reflect heterogeneous ice growth and altered energy redistribution within nanoscale ice domains, implying that yields measured on planar substrates may substantially overestimate photodesorption from the thin ice mantles of cosmic dust.

2611.08539.abstract: Weekly detection forecasts could help prioritize fire monitoring across Bolivia. We estimate the probability of at least one fire detection by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite in each 0.05-degree cell during the following 7 days. Primary models were fixed before test scoring. Calibrated LightGBM, a gradient-boosted decision-tree model, reaches 2023-2025 temporal-test average precision (AP) of 0.323 (95% block-bootstrap interval 0.222-0.383), compared with 0.167 for climatology and 0.143 for persistence. Its paired AP gain over climatology is 0.1567 (0.0998-0.2179). A separately selected geographic model reaches AP 0.384 versus 0.181 for persistence in regions excluded from fitting. In the temporal-test population, reviewing the highest-ranked 5% and 10% of eligible area would have covered 38.4% and 55.8% of cell-weeks with detections. Probabilities still overestimate detection frequency in the highest-probability group. Retrospective rainfall provides no clear AP improvement; the primary validation comparisons for vegetation, land cover and their combination are inconclusive. Positive secondary or exploratory intervals do not change those decisions. Evaluation requires complete target and recent-history observations and measures satellite detections, not individual fires, causes or burned area. Prospective evaluation should archive inputs at each weekly issue and measure ranking, calibration and the usefulness of selected cells for monitoring decisions.

2611.08583.abstract: To use a dark-matter model one needs to know what defines it, which observables it affects, which codes and likelihoods evaluate it, and under what assumptions a published bound applies. That information is scattered across tens of thousands of papers. We present DarkMatterFM-Registry, a machine-readable registry of dark-matter models extracted from arXiv full texts by a staged large-language-model (LLM) pipeline: 6,145 structured model cards, validated against a seven-file JSON Schema suite, ranked by expected value for observational follow-up, and enriched for the top ~2,000 with observables, constraints, and theory-to-observable routes. Schema checks pass 97.8% of cards, and an LLM-judged accuracy study on a stratified card sample finds 81% of section verdicts correct, 18% partially correct, and none hallucinated. As a first application we turn the registry into a priority-weighted roadmap of 25 concrete projects the community could build. The roadmap is built by judging every computational step of every enriched model's theory-to-observable routes as available, partial, or missing, and aggregating the resulting typed gaps weighted by model priority. We find that what blocks the most high-priority models is not missing theory but missing shared infrastructure: model files for existing relic-abundance solvers, a general non-cold Boltzmann-code framework, reusable indirect-detection likelihoods, and a Lyman-$\alpha$ forest likelihood for non-cold dark matter (the largest gap for structure-formation probes). The model cards, schemas, roadmap, and ranking are released making the project reproducible and the cards available for the community.

2611.08596.abstract: The upcoming Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is expected to be sensitive to thousands of white dwarf (WD) binaries in our galaxy, extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) of stellar-mass compact objects into massive black holes, stellar-mass black hole binaries (SOBHBs) in their early inspiral phase, and, crucially, massive black hole binaries (MBHBs) with masses in the range of $10^4$-$10^7 M_\odot$. The presence of such a large number of signals requires joint inference of all parameters across all sources present in the data, an approach referred to as "global fit". This requires evaluating hundreds of thousands of waveform templates, which can be computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we present $\texttt{Phentax}$, a $\texttt{JAX}$ re-implementation of the $\texttt{IMRPhenomTHM}$ waveform model. This is a state-of-the-art time-domain phenomenological waveform model for comparable-mass binary black holes that includes the effects of higher-order modes. Given this, $\texttt{IMRPhenomTHM}$ is one of the models currently used to simulate and analyze MBHB signals in LISA. With $\texttt{Phentax}$, we provide a fast, easy-to-batch, and differentiable implementation of this waveform model to accelerate the development of LISA global fit algorithms.

2611.08824.abstract: Since their pioneer observations more than thirty years ago, exoplanets have been a major topic among the astrophysics community. Despite their ubiquity, our knowledge of planetary parameters and internal compositions still mostly relies on stellar quantities estimated through evolutionary models, which suffer from a calibration bias, preventing the community to have accurate discussions on the diversity of planets across the Universe. We use our sample to demonstrate the current best reachable precision of the CHARA Array to be $\sim$ 2% on radius determination, with an error budget dominated by the uncertainty on the angular diameter, while systematics are shown to be of the order of 1% thanks to our methodology. While the precision matches values found in the literature, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the present study in the relevance of the results put forward. Finally, we show that our methods naturally translate into an improved accuracy of the planetary parameters, along with an improvement in precision by $\sim$ 50% in radius and $\sim$ 30% in mass.

2611.08880.title: A pipeline for identifying astrophysical signals and instrumental glitches in LISA data

figures.caption: Figure 1: A flowchart describing our proposed pipeline for transient search and classification for LISA. The pipeline consists of two parts: a search algorithm and a machine learning classifier. The former takes as input, the LISA TDI channels (Section I.2). It divides this data into 6 hour segments and generates Q-transforms (Section III.1) of each. Any excess of energy is classified as a transient (Section III.2) and the Q-transforms containing transients are passed on to the classifier (Section IV.2).The classifier is a CNN that processes each input image and outputs two scores: its confidence that a GW is present and its confidence that a glitch is present. The scores each range from 0 to 1 with a higher number indicating a greater likelihood of the corresponding transient type being present in the image.

Figure 2: The two panels on the left show $$$Q$$$-transform representations with different Q values of the same GW and glitch simulation (see Section II). It can be seen that a lower Q value, better represents shorter duration transients (glitch at $t=7$ hours in this case). On the other hand, longer duration transients (GW merging close to $t=5$ hours) are better represented by higher Q values. The red contours divide areas where the energy (Equation 11) is greater than 8 and less than 8. The rightmost panel displays a histogram of the time distribution for all triggers in both images overlaid with the Gaussian KDE. Note that the histogram had no role in computing the KDE and is simply shown for comparison. Peaks with a prominence exceeding 0.05 in density are identified as transients, and the times at which they occur are recorded as transients.

The classifier takes as input, images $w$ith a shape of $128\times 128\times 4$ and outputs a $2\times 1$ column vector containing the scores for each transient being present in the image. For a given transient, a score of 1 indicates presence and a score of 0 indicates absence. The shapes of the output of each layer is also shown where w is a variable hyperparameter. 2611.08880.abstract: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is a space-based gravitational wave detector scheduled for launch in the 2030s by the European Space Agency. Operating in the 0.1 mHz to 0.1 Hz band, LISA will observe a variety of astrophysical sources including but not limited to supermassive black hole mergers, extreme mass ratio inspirals, and white dwarf binaries. LISA will yield new insights, including supermassive black hole formation, new tests of general relativity, population studies of white dwarfs and others. Like all interferometric gravitational wave detectors, LISA data is expected to contain non-astrophysical transients, commonly referred to as glitches. We introduce a two step pipeline that consists of a search algorithm for detecting potential transients in simulated LISA data followed by a machine learning model that classifies the detected transients as gravitational waves or instrumental glitches. This is important for MBHBs with very high masses (around $10^6\ M_{\odot}$) which are transients that could be morphologically similar to LISA glitches in the data. Initial results demonstrate a promising ability to classify detected events with an accuracy close to $98\%$. The pipeline also shows the ability to analyze a month of data in under 2 minutes on a laptop. This shows an eventual utility of our pipeline for enabling accurate rapid alerts from low latency searches. It could also support model selection in global-fit analyses by providing an initial summary of the location and type of individual signals. This paper also discusses challenges encountered during training, including limitations of the current framework.

The lighter colored points indicate planets with radii within 5% of the non-inflated models ($R_{\rm obs}\leq 1.05\,R_{\epsilon=0}$), which are not included in the fits. The dashed lines show $x=y$. In the x-axis labels, $M_{\rm P}$ and $R_{\rm P}$ are in Jupiter units, $\epsilon\pi R_{\rm P}^{2}F_{\rm irr}$ in units of $\mathrm{L_{J}}$, and $F_{\rm irr}$ in units of $10^{9}$ erg cm-2 s-1. The fitted coefficients and their uncertainties are given in Table 1.

Figure 6: Comparison of our interpolated magnetic field estimates and indirect magnetic field constraints reported in the literature. We show $2B_{\rm dip,surf}$ when comparing with the Vidotto et al. (2010); Cauley et al. (2019) and Turner et al. (2021) SPI estimates, and $10B_{\rm dip,surf}$ when comparing with the Seidel et al. (2026) atmospheric maximum estimations (see text). Both the exoplanetary parameters and the magnetic estimates are shown in App. F.

Figure 7: Comparison between the $B_{\rm rms,dyn}$ values predicted by the Reiners et al. (2009) scaling law (x-axis) and the interpolated ones (y-axis) for each planet. For the R09 prediction, we assume that the internal luminosity is equal to the total injected heating power, $L_{\rm P}=\epsilon\pi R_{\rm P}^{2}F_{\rm irr}$, as in Yadav & Thorngren (2017). The dashed line indicates perfect agreement with the R09 prediction.

Figure 8: Interpolated heating efficiencies for the internal heat deposition mechanism, $\epsilon_{\rm inner}$, as a function of incident stellar flux. Marker size scales with $R_{\rm P}^{2}$. The dashed line shows the $\epsilon_{\rm Th18}$ relation from Thorngren & Fortney (2018) (Eq. 17).

2611.09128.abstract: Hot Jupiters (HJs) are commonly thought to host the strongest dynamo-generated magnetic fields among exoplanets, exceeding Jupiter's by up to an order of magnitude, which can potentially induce observable star-planet interaction (SPI) and planetary radio emission. However, while several indirect, model-dependent estimates of HJ magnetic fields have been reported from SPIs and recent transmission spectroscopy diagnostics, no unambiguous direct (radio) detection has yet been achieved. We aim to provide a range of magnetic field estimates for HJs, considering the mechanisms responsible for inflation and the convective flux entering the magnetic field scaling law. Given that their dynamos operate in the fast-rotating regime (Rossby number <~ 0.1), we combine one-dimensional evolutionary interior models with magnetic field scaling laws under two limiting heating scenarios: deep and shallow energy depositions. The deep-heating scenario maximizes convective heat flux in the dynamo and predicts strong magnetic fields of up to ~100 G, whereas shallow heating, which is arguably more realistic for most proposed physical mechanisms, weakens convection and yields much weaker fields of O(1) G. The strong field scenario is compatible with SPI indirect detections, and the weak field scenario is in agreement with recent atmospheric constraints. We derive scaling law relations based on observables (planetary mass, radius, and/or incident stellar flux): Bstrong = 19 M_P^0.6 R_P^1.7 G; Bweak = 0.8 M_P^1.5 R_P^-1.2 G. These predictions provide a framework for interpreting future atmospheric wind measurements, SPI signatures, and radio observations, which may ultimately discriminate between competing interior-heating scenarios.

2611.09198.title: New optimisations for exact, scalable 2D Gaussian process inference, with applications to astronomical time-series

figures.caption: Figure 1: Runtime to decompose matrices using an M4 MacBook Air and an NVIDIA A100 GPU for eigendecomposition (using jax.numpy.linalg.eigh), general Cholesky decomposition (using jax.scipy.linalg.cholesky), and quasiseparable Cholesky decomposition of an exponential kernel (using tinygp). The GPU is typically slower for small matrices, but outperforms the CPU for larger matrices by exploiting more parallel workers.

Figure 2: Simulated spectroscopic time-series of an exoplanet eclipse with measurement covariance added following the kernel function given in Equation 19. Note the vertical streaks in the residuals which resemble real JWST/NIRCam data reductions, such as in Ahrer et al., (2023). Despite simulating with very low white noise, the white light curve appears particularly noisy (compare with Figures 3, 4, 5 which have the same amplitude of white noise), a consequence of how wavelength correlations bin down gradually compared to white noise.

Figure 3: Same as Figure 2 but injecting a stellar granulation signal following the kernel in Equation 20. The wavelength-dependence $\alpha(\lambda)$ follows the model in Morris et al., (2020) with an arbitrary scaling, while the time-dependence is stochastic and follows an exponential kernel in time. The systematics have the same shape in all light curves, but their amplitude is largest at optical wavelengths and gradually weakens into near-infrared wavelengths.

Figure 4: Analogous plot to Figure 3 but with the kernel function flipped, injecting a low-rank term whose amplitude follows a deterministic exponential decay in time, but treating the amplitude in wavelength as a GP following a squared exponential kernel. An example use case is fitting spectroscopic light curves with wavelength-dependent settling, imposing that the settling amplitude varies gradually between wavelengths as a GP, but still explicitly defining how the settling varies in time within the function $\beta(t)$. Adding this term to the GP covariance matrix allows us to analytically marginalise out the wavelength-dependent settling amplitude.

Figure 5: Similar to Figures 2, 3, and 4, but with systematics simulated using a 2D kernel term (a squared exponential in wavelength times an exponential kernel in time), with a short wavelength length scale to simulate systematics that are close to independent for each light curve. This is similar to what is currently modelled when fitting a GP to each spectroscopic light curve independently. The height scale could also be varied in wavelength, in case there are specific wavelengths with strong systematics.

Figure 7: The MultiLowRankKernel can separate low-rank components based on different time correlations, while PCA can struggle to distinguish them when they have a similar amplitude. The left plot shows simulated systematics generated with a sum of $N_{\alpha}=2$ low-rank kernel terms, an exponential time kernel with a constant $100$ ppm amplitude in wavelength, and a simple harmonic oscillator time kernel with wavelength amplitudes $\bm{\alpha}_{\lambda}$ varying linearly from 172 ppm to -172 ppm (i.e. it is anti-correlated between the top and bottom light curves, and zero in the middle light curve). The time-dependence of the injected signals is overplotted in grey in both the middle and right plots (with a rescaling applied): the two largest PCA components recover a mixture of these two signals as they have similar amplitudes (middle plot), while the best-fit MultiLowRankKernel model fits for the wavelength-dependence of these components and separates their time-dependence almost exactly (right plot), visualised using the transformed residuals $\tilde{\mathbf{r}}=\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{transf}}^{-1}\mathbf{r}$, as this projects each systematics component onto separate light curves.

Figure 8: Left: $N$umber of eigenvalues $\lambda>10^{-12}$ for a covariance matrix built using a squared exponential kernel on N regularly sampled input locations, with $h=1$ and length scale given relative to the full input range. Longer length scales result in very few significant eigenvectors. Right: Nine most significant eigenvectors for the case of $N=256$ and length scale equal to the input range. The square root of the eigenvalue $\sqrt{\lambda}$ gives the standard deviation of the Gaussian prior placed on that eigenvector by the GP log-likelihood.

Figure D1: GP regression and prediction requires the training points $\mathbf{y}$ to lie on a complete input grid, which is satisfied in the left and middle plots, but not the rightmost plot. The prediction locations $\mathbf{y}_{*}$ are not required to lie on a grid, but we do require the combined training and prediction locations to lie on a grid, which all plots satisfy.

Figure D2: We can always train on a grid of locations and predict values on a different input grid, even though the union of these points doesn’t form a grid directly. We do this by predicting at additional locations, so that the union of trained and predicted points forms a complete grid. We can then simply discard these additional predicted values.

2611.09198.abstract:
Astronomical datasets often consist of a grid of datapoints in two or more dimensions, such as images, spectroscopic time-series, and imaging time-series. Gaussian processes (GPs) are a powerful tool for dealing with correlated noise in these data, arising from both astrophysical and instrumental systematics. Despite this, popular GP optimisations such as celerite are largely restricted to 1D datasets. Extensions to 2D data typically come with limited flexibility or poor scaling. As a motivating example, this limitation is significant for transiting exoplanet spectroscopy with JWST, as current analyses typically assume each spectroscopic light curve is statistically independent, despite many potential sources of wavelength-correlation, including detector readout noise and stellar granulation. This introduces a potential bias in atmospheric retrievals which is typically ignored.
To solve this problem, we present new, exact GP optimisations implemented in the JAX-based package luas, which extend 1D GP optimisations to multidimensional data using Kronecker product algebra. These GP optimisations are highly flexible, permit efficient analysis of 2D datasets containing millions of datapoints, and in many cases have a cheaper cost than transit light curve modelling. These optimisations are key to pushing the limits of exoplanet spectroscopy to smaller targets around bright host stars, as we increasingly hit instrumental and astrophysical noise floors. We suggest further applications to the analysis of ground-based high resolution spectroscopic time-series, extreme precision radial velocities, and high-contrast imaging, drawing on the connection that certain 2D GP models represent a probabilistic generalisation of PCA. Applications may even extend to machine learning and geostatistics, as we present novel optimisations for the Linear Mixing Model and the Linear Model of Coregionalisation.

2611.09827.title: Effects of a Nuclear Detonation in Low Earth Orbit

figures.caption: Figure 1: Burst location changes the geometry and intensity of the artificial radiation belt. Peak shell-average dose rate behind 2 mm of aluminium after a 1-Mt detonation, shown in the magnetic meridian of each burst for the central source of 1.29 emitted electrons per fission before trapping. (a) A burst at 485 km over $40.75^{\circ}$N, $35.5^{\circ}$W, selected near the highest instantaneous satellite density in the January catalogue to maximize prompt exposure. (b) A burst at 500 km over $20^{\circ}$S, $35^{\circ}$W, near the South Atlantic Anomaly, selected to produce an intense belt overlapping populated LEO altitudes. Red crosses mark the burst locations; red shading illustrates the approximately 2,400-km vacuum range within which prompt X-ray fluence exceeds the adopted 40 J m-2 failure threshold 10. The blue band marks 200–2000-km altitudes, and black curves show $L=2$ and $L=3$. The display uses a centered-dipole projection; injection shells, trapping and belt intensities use IGRF-14 for 14 January 2026 16. The burst in (a) populates shells $L=1.74$–2.19, with a peak dose rate of approximately 12 rad s-1; the burst in (b) populates more compact shells, $L=1.31$–1.51, producing a peak of approximately 30 rad s-1.

Figure 2: Burst location determines whether electrons remain trapped and the intensity of the resulting belt. Peak shell-average dose rate behind 2 mm of aluminium as a function of burst latitude and longitude for a 1-Mt detonation at 500 km, using the central source of 1.29 emitted electrons per fission and IGRF-14 for 14 January 2026 16. White contours mark 1, 10, 20 and 30 rad s-1; uncolored cells lie below the displayed 0.1 rad s-1 limit or outside the calculation domain. For bursts near the magnetic equator over parts of the Indian Ocean and Indonesia, injected electrons reach shells whose mirror points descend below the 120-km atmospheric boundary over the South Atlantic Anomaly, preventing persistent trapping. This loss along the full drift path is accounted for through the drift loss cone 19, 12. Injection over the South Atlantic can instead populate compact shells overlapping LEO, producing particularly intense belts. The cross marks the reference burst at $20^{\circ}$S, $35^{\circ}$W over the South Atlantic Anomaly.

Figure 3: Repeated exposure to the artificial belt disables nearly the entire modeled fleet. (a) Cumulative fraction of the 13,306-object fleet disabled after a 1-Mt detonation at 500 km over $20^{\circ}$S, $35^{\circ}$W, for a 40 krad(Si) failure threshold behind 2 mm of aluminium. The line denotes the central source of 1.29 emitted electrons per fission; shading spans the lower and upper sources of 0.40 and 5.21, each combined with the calculated trapping efficiency. Electron counts are derived from beta-activity histories calculated with ONIX 15. Prompt X-rays disable 2.9% at $t=0$. Numbered markers identify the snapshots in (b). (b) Fleet status at 0, 1, 3 and 7 days in the central source case, with satellite positions propagated to each snapshot time. Gray denotes operational objects and red denotes radiation-disabled objects. Losses rise from approximately 3% initially to 25%, 78% and 98%, respectively. Results for both tolerance thresholds and all three source cases are given in Supplementary Table S2.

Figure 4: Radiation failures produce an early collision surge followed by altitude-dependent clearance. Results for a 1-Mt detonation at 500 km over $20^{\circ}$S, $35^{\circ}$W, with the central electron source and a uniform 40 krad(Si) threshold behind 2 mm of aluminium. (a) Avoidance-modified global CRASH Clock, the inverse instantaneous expected collision rate across all modeled pairs, including catastrophic and cratering outcomes, rocket-body encounters and debris–debris impacts 13. Small plots show the clock during the first 15 days and the cumulative probability of at least one collision. The dashed line marks the initial no-maneuvering reference calculated using the same catalogue and geometric cross-sections. (b) Cumulative expected satellite–satellite and satellite–debris collisions. Rocket-body and debris–debris encounters contribute to the reported totals but are omitted from this panel. (c) Intact radiation-disabled payloads, pre-existing catalogued debris and new collision fragments, weighted by the fraction of each orbit spent below 2000 km. Debris counts refer to characteristic lengths of at least 10 cm. Solid curves in (a)–(c) use the central solar-flux path; shading spans results from the NASA/MSFC 5th- and 95th-percentile paths, which alter atmospheric density and drag. These ranges show sensitivity to atmospheric forcing, not statistical confidence intervals. (d) Expected pre-existing debris and new fragments per 50-km altitude band, shown in grayscale and color, respectively. Both distributions use logarithmic scales spanning 1–2000 objects per band. New fragments receive breakup velocity kicks, and both debris populations move between altitudes under orbit-averaged drag 14, 21. Geometric cross-sections and masses depend on object class and Starlink generation. Atmospheric forcing follows the NASA/MSFC solar-flux paths and CIRA density profiles 22, 23; model assumptions are detailed in Methods.

Figure S1: Altitude distribution of the objects used for the radiation calculation. Counts of the 13,306 selected objects at 08:00 UTC on 14 January 2026, propagated from the retained CelesTrak elements 1. Bars use 25-km bins; the blue band highlights 500–600 km. Altitude is evaluated at the burst time.

Figure S2: Altitude and time determine the relative collision hazard for an inserted satellite. Instantaneous rate for a payload in a circular orbit divided by its rate in the matched no-detonation model. Both calculations use the same $9\times 2.8\times 0.2$-m geometric proxy. (a) Non-maneuvering payload, with avoidance credit only against operational partners. (b) Maneuvering payload, with an assumed 99% avoidance benefit against every modeled partner. Blue denotes a ratio below one and red above one; white denotes equal rates. Triangular color-bar extensions mark values outside 0.01–100. Gray cells, if present, have no positive control rate. Both models use the January inventory, central solar forcing and identical test geometry. Radiation failure of the test payload and debris below 10 cm are excluded. Rates below the control reflect fewer collision targets and do not establish that operations could safely resume.

2611.09827.abstract: More than 13,000 satellites operate in low Earth orbit (LEO), and concern has grown that nuclear weapons could be used in space to target them. Beyond the initial X-ray burst, electrons released by radioactive fission products can become trapped in Earth's magnetic field, repeatedly exposing satellites as an artificial radiation belt. Here we couple prompt radiation, electron trapping and belt evolution to satellite failures, collisions and atmospheric drag. For a 1-Mt detonation at 500km over the South Atlantic, repeated belt exposure disables approximately 98% of modeled satellites within one week in our central case. Tripling the assumed radiation tolerance delays widespread failure by only days: approximately 97% are still disabled within two weeks. The loss of maneuverability sharply increases collision risk, with approximately 20 collisions expected within two years. Drag removes many disabled spacecraft from lower altitudes, but replacement satellites could remain exposed to radiation and debris for years. These findings show how a single detonation could devastate orbital infrastructure and support efforts to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.
